title: Satan “came also among them” — is he one of the sons of God, and by what standing does he come before the Lord?
summary: Twice Satan comes before the Lord with the sons of God, is questioned, and is given power over Job within limits. The passage does not say whether he is one of the sons of God, what his office is, or why he is admitted.
text: KJV Job 1:6: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:6: וַיָּבֹ֥וא גַֽם־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן בְּתֹוכָֽם; the word is written with the article prefixed. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:6: καὶ ὁ διάβολος ἦλθε μετʼ αὐτῶν. [and the devil came with them]. KJV 1:7: “Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the Lord, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” KJV 1:12: “Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord.” KJV 2:1: “and Satan came also among them to present himself before the Lord” KJV 2:6: “And the Lord said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life.” KJV 2:7: “So went Satan forth from the presence of the Lord, and smote Job with sore boils” Other places where the KJV Old Testament has the name: 1 Chronicles 21:1: “And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.” Psalms 109:6: “and let Satan stand at his right hand” Zechariah 3:1: “and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him” Zechariah 3:2: “The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan” KJV Revelation 12:10: “for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm.
reasoning: The verses quoted state what Satan does: he comes on the day the sons of God come, says he has been going to and fro in the earth, challenges the Lord about Job, is twice given leave with a limit, and goes out from the presence of the Lord. They do not state what he is. “Among them” can be read as one of their number or as one who came in beside them; “also” can be read either way. The matter bears on how the whole account is read: whether Job’s losses come from a servant of the heavenly court doing a task, or from an enemy of God who is allowed to act.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that Satan is here one of the sons of God whose part is to accuse or test; that he is an adversary of God who comes in uninvited or by permission; and that the word is a title for an office, not a name. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV, the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. The Greek word differs from the KJV’s name, and the Greek of 1:6 calls the others angels; neither says whether he is one of them. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV Old Testament was searched for the word “Satan” outside Job (four verses: 1 Chronicles 21:1; Psalms 109:6; Zechariah 3:1 and 3:2) and all four were read; Revelation 12:9–10 was read as well. Zechariah shows Satan standing to resist a man before the angel of the Lord and being rebuked, and Revelation speaks of an accuser before God who is cast down; neither says what his standing was in the scene of Job 1 and 2. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The Hebrew and Greek of the verses outside Job were not compared. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: “There was a man in the land of Uz” — where was Uz, and when did Job live?
summary: The book opens with a man in the land of Uz, the greatest of the men of the east. The opening names no king, no year, no father and no people for him. Brenton’s Greek adds a passage at the end of the book that gives a place, a line of descent and another name; the Hebrew and the KJV have no such passage.
text: KJV Job 1:1: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: אִ֛ישׁ הָיָ֥ה בְאֶֽרֶץ־ע֖וּץ אִיֹּ֣וב שְׁמֹ֑ו. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:1: ἌΝΘΡΩΠΟΣ τις ἦν ἐν χώρᾳ τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰὼβ. KJV 1:3: “so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east” The name Uz elsewhere in the KJV. Genesis 10:23: “And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.” Genesis 36:28: “The children of Dishan are these; Uz, and Aran.” Jeremiah 25:20: “and all the kings of the land of Uz” Lamentations 4:21: “O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz” Job named elsewhere. Ezekiel 14:14: “Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it” James 5:11: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job” The end of the book. KJV Job 42:17: “So Job died, being old and full of days.” Brenton’s Greek prints 42:17 and then five lettered verses, 17a to 17e, which the Hebrew edition and the KJV do not have. 17b: Οὗτος ἑρμηνεύεται ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου, ἐν μὲν γῇ κατοικῶν τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ἐπὶ τοῖς ὁρίοις τῆς Ἰδουμαίας καὶ Ἀραβίας· προϋπῆρχε δὲ αὐτῷ ὄνομα Ἰωβάβ· [This man is interpreted out of the Syriac book as dwelling in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia; and his name before was Jobab]. 17c, in part: ὥστε εἶναι αὐτὸν πέμπτον ἀπὸ Ἁβραάμ· [so that he was the fifth from Abraam]. KJV Genesis 36:33 has a Jobab among the kings of Edom: “Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB42.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew the opening places Job by one name of a land and by the phrase “the men of the east”, and gives no reign, generation or kindred by which to date him. The other KJV verses that have the name Uz use it of a son of Aram, of a son of Dishan, of a land with kings (Jeremiah), and of a land where the daughter of Edom dwells (Lamentations); none of them mentions Job. Where and when Job lived bears on how his sacrifices, his knowledge of God and the book’s relation to Israel are read.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The gap is in the Hebrew edition and the KJV. The Greek edition quoted does state an answer, in a passage after 42:17 that says it is drawn from “the Syriac book”: it places the land on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia, gives Job an earlier name, Jobab, and makes him fifth from Abraham. Whether that passage is right, and whether the Jobab of Genesis 36:33 is the same man, are not established by the verses quoted, and this record asserts neither. Possible readings: that Job lived in the time of the patriarchs; that he was an Edomite; that Uz lay toward Aram; and that the book does not mean to fix a time. Each is an interpretation. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for the word “Uz” (seven verses: Genesis 10:23 and 36:28; 1 Chronicles 1:17 and 1:42; Job 1:1; Jeremiah 25:20; Lamentations 4:21) and all were read; Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11 were read as well. None of these gives a date or a kindred for Job. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. The other lettered verses of the Greek ending were not compared with Genesis 36 here. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “I know that my redeemer liveth” — who is the redeemer Job means?
summary: Job says he knows that his redeemer lives and will stand upon the earth. The verse does not say who the redeemer is. In the same speech Job says the hand of God has touched him, and in the next verse that he will see God.
text: KJV Job 19:25: “For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:” Hebrew (WLC) 19:25: וַאֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי גֹּ֣אֲלִי חָ֑י. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 19:25: Οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι ἀένναός ἐστιν ὁ ἐκλύειν με μέλλων, [For I know that he is everlasting who is about to release me,] KJV 19:21: “for the hand of God hath touched me” KJV 19:26: “yet in my flesh shall I see God” Earlier in Job’s speeches. KJV 9:33: “Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both.” KJV 16:19: “Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high.” KJV 16:21: “O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man pleadeth for his neighbour!” The word elsewhere in the KJV. Proverbs 23:11: “For their redeemer is mighty; he shall plead their cause with thee.” Isaiah 44:6: “Thus saith the Lord the King of Israel, and his redeemer the Lord of hosts” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/19/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB19.htm.
reasoning: The verse names the redeemer only by what he is to Job. The chapter gives two things that pull apart: God is the one whose hand has touched Job (19:21), and God is the one Job will see (19:26). Earlier Job has said that there is no daysman between him and God (9:33) and that he has a witness in heaven (16:19), and has wished that one might plead for a man with God (16:21). Whether the redeemer of 19:25 is God himself, the witness of 16:19, or someone else is not said. The answer decides whether Job here appeals to God against God’s own treatment of him, or to another.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the redeemer is God; that he is a heavenly witness or advocate other than God; that he is a human kinsman or vindicator; and that he is the Christ of the New Testament. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV, the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. The Greek words for the redeemer differ from the KJV’s and name no one either. Isaiah 44:6 calls the Lord the redeemer of Israel and Proverbs 23:11 speaks of a redeemer of the fatherless; a shared word does not settle whom Job means. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for the word “redeemer” (eighteen verses, of which Job 19:25 is the only one in Job); Proverbs 23:11 and Isaiah 44:6 were read, the others were not read for this record. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. A separate record compares the Greek wording of 19:25–26 with the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
